principles.text: Be wary of stocks rallying straight up into daily/weekly resistance while their EMAs are still trending lower — that kind of move is a red flag, not a buy signal.
If a stock you're watching (or holding) starts losing the rising 9 or 21 EMA, treat that as a huge red flag — it invalidates the setup.

When the general market/indices are extended, it's much harder to find a tight-risk entry on strength — always time individual entries against the health/extension of the broader market, not just the setup in isolation.

No risk, no reward — don't let fear of stopping out or taking a loss cause you to skip good opportunities; take the trade while price is still holding the key level (the invalidation point hasn't hit yet), and if it fails, accept it and re-evaluate.

Decide whether you'll take a breakout before it actually happens — commit to pressing the buy button immediately at the breakout candle rather than waiting 15-20 seconds to confirm, which lowers reaction time and often means chasing.
It's possible to enter before a key-level bounce is confirmed (before the candle even closes), but expect a meaningfully lower win rate for doing so.

When you have a recurring trading problem (e.g. overtrading, entering too many positions at once), diagnose the actual root cause first — is it mental discomfort with size, poor execution, or FOMO/revenge trading — rather than looking for a generic fix.
If you keep getting stopped out repeatedly, drill down into why: are you entering at the wrong time, is the entry itself not optimal, or are you entering somewhat randomly without a clear plan.

None of your biggest/best trades will come from revenge trading during a difficult, losing period — statistically it's undeniable that the best trades never come from those emotional, revenge-driven stretches.
You can't fully eliminate FOMO or revenge trading, but you can gradually reduce it over time through hard lessons and drawdowns — improvement is incremental, not a single fix.

Accept that overnight/gap risk is part of the game — you can't control whether a position gaps up or down, so embrace the uncertainty rather than dwelling on the downside ('never met a successful pessimist').

Before going full-time on trading: build roughly 2 years of consistent track record spanning different market conditions (uptrend, sideways, downtrend), have trading income that clearly exceeds (ideally 2-3x) your day-job income, and keep a financial cushion of at least 6-12 months of expenses.

If you have to ask other people (or discuss with family/friends) whether you're ready to quit your job and trade full-time, you're not ready — when you truly are ready, you'll know it with certainty rather than being 90% sure.
